common_name: Fascination Hosta (Historic Cream-Streaked Green Hosta, Parent of Flamboyant and Shade Fanfare)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fascination is an older Paul Aden-bred hosta valued today chiefly as the streaked parent behind the popular sport 'Flamboyant', which in turn gave rise to 'Shade Fanfare'.

directions: Fascination is an early Paul Aden hosta introduction grown today mainly for its place in hosta breeding history rather than as a common garden plant in its own right, having given rise to the widely grown streaked sport 'Flamboyant,' which in turn produced the classic cream-edged 'Shade Fanfare.' Its heart-shaped green leaves carry irregular creamy-white streaking that varies from leaf to leaf, a less stable and less uniform pattern than the bolder, more defined variegation of its later sports. Like other streaked hostas it is prone to reverting toward solid green or throwing more heavily variegated shoots, so periodically divide out and discard reverted growth to keep a planting looking its best. Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade, with a little morning sun helping to hold the cream streaking, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Paradise Island Hosta (Gold-Centered Green-Margined Hosta with Red Petioles)

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring, setting the crown at the depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Paradise Island is a Hans Hansen-bred hosta from the 'Paradise' series and is the parent of the smaller gold-and-green sport 'Island Breeze'.

directions: Paradise Island bears thick, rounded, gold-centered leaves broadly margined in dark green, with distinctive red-speckled petioles that echo the coloring shared across Hans Hansen's 'Paradise' series and carry through into its own sport, 'Island Breeze.' Brighter light intensifies the gold leaf center while deeper shade shifts the color toward chartreuse, so morning sun with afternoon shade brings out the best two-tone contrast. Lavender, bell-shaped flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich soil, mulch to conserve moisture through summer heat, and divide congested clumps only occasionally, since this cultivar builds a full clump slowly.

common_name: Europa Daylily (Historic Sterile Triploid 'Ditch Lily' Clone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in average to poor soil in full sun to light shade; 'Europa' is the sterile triploid clone of tawny daylily that early colonists carried to North America and that later spread along roadsides and old homesites as the familiar orange 'ditch lily.'

directions: Europa is the specific triploid clone of tawny daylily, Hemerocallis fulva, that was carried from Europe by early colonists and subsequently spread across North America by division and by roadside plantings, becoming the ubiquitous orange 'ditch lily' seen along highways, fencerows, and abandoned home sites. As a sterile triploid it sets essentially no viable seed, spreading instead by vigorous underground rhizomes that let a single planting expand into large colonies over the years, useful for erosion control on slopes but requiring firm edging or a root barrier in a mixed border. Arlow Stout used Europa as a key foundation parent in his pioneering daylily breeding work at the New York Botanical Garden, including the historic dark red cultivar 'Theron.' Its tawny orange, trumpet-shaped flowers open for a single day in a heavy midsummer flush; established plantings need essentially no care and tolerate poor soil, drought, and heavy competition better than almost any modern hybrid daylily.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database
New York Botanical Garden — Arlow Stout Daylily Research Archives

common_name: Petite Embers Crape Myrtle (True Dwarf Red-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Petite Embers is part of the true-dwarf Petite breeding series developed by Carl Whitcomb specifically for small-space and container use, staying far smaller than standard landscape crape myrtles.

directions: Petite Embers is a true dwarf crape myrtle from the Petite breeding series developed by Carl Whitcomb, staying under 4 feet tall at maturity, far smaller than the tree-form National Arboretum cultivars that dominate most crape myrtle plantings. It bears clusters of watermelon-red to deep pink flowers through summer on a dense, compact, well-branched shrub sized for foundation plantings, low borders, and large containers where full-size crape myrtles would quickly outgrow the space. Like other crape myrtles it flowers on new wood, so any shaping should be done in late winter before spring growth begins rather than after flower buds have set. Water regularly through the first growing season to establish a deep root system; once established it tolerates heat and drought with only occasional deep watering.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivar Selection

common_name: Tampa Grape Rootstock (Pierce's Disease-Tolerant Florida Bunch Grape Understock)

planting.note: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired bunch grape variety onto the young rootstock; Tampa was developed at the University of Florida specifically to give Pierce's disease tolerance to grafted bunch grapes such as Orlando Seedless grown in the humid, leafhopper-prone Deep South and Florida.

directions: Tampa is a rootstock selection bred at the University of Florida's grape breeding program specifically to address Pierce's disease, the bacterial infection spread by glassy-winged sharpshooters and other leafhoppers that has historically made growing many bunch grape varieties on their own roots impractical across Florida and the Gulf South. Grafted onto Tampa, susceptible fruiting cultivars such as Orlando Seedless gain meaningfully better tolerance of Pierce's disease along with the vigor needed to perform in Florida's warm, humid growing conditions and sandy native soils. It is used alongside the similarly bred Dog Ridge (Dogridge) rootstock as one of the standard understock choices for Florida bunch grape production, with growers choosing between the two largely on vigor and soil-type compatibility rather than fruit-quality differences, since the rootstock itself bears no fruit of horticultural interest. Bench-graft or bud a named bunch grape cultivar onto young Tampa rootstock in late winter or spring, and grow on in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Grape Breeding and Rootstock Program
